I therefore assume the signal triggers the purchase and the position is then held continuously; exits, taxes, fees and dividends are excluded. A strategy that sells after an opposite crossover cannot be valued without knowing the future sequence of signals.

Compound interest is what happens when the interest you earn on an investment starts earning interest of its own. Think of it as "interest on interest." Instead of just earning a flat return on your original money year after year, your returns get added to the pot, and the next round of growth is calculated on that larger total.

Here's a simple way to picture it: If you put $100 in an account earning 10% per year, after one year you have $110. In year two, you earn 10% on the full $110, not just the original $100, so you get $121. That extra dollar is compound interest at work. Over time, this snowball effect can make your money grow much faster than simple interest, which only pays on the original amount.

The two big levers are **time** and **rate**. The longer your money stays invested, the more dramatic the compounding becomes. Even a small difference in the annual return can lead to a surprisingly large difference after many years. A classic rule of thumb is the Rule of 72: divide 72 by your annual return to get a rough estimate of how many years it takes for your money to double.

If you're curious to see this in action, you could look up a compound interest calculator online and play with different starting amounts, time horizons, and rates. A nearby historical experiment: try plugging in the long-term average return of a broad stock market index (roughly 7–10% before inflation) and see what a small monthly contribution might grow to over 30 years.

prose_judge.notes: The reply provides a clear, honest explanation of compound interest without any unsupported capability claims or raw runtime errors. It uses a simple example and the Rule of 72, and appropriately suggests using an external calculator rather than promising to perform the computation itself.

Un ETF (Exchange Traded Fund) es un fondo cotizado en bolsa que agrupa activos como acciones, bonos o materias primas y se negocia como una acción individual. Ofrece diversificación sencilla y bajos costos. En Argus puedes probar estrategias buy_and_hold o DCA con ETFs como SPY.

Yes, you can absolutely use Bollinger Bands in a rule.  

Bollinger Bands are one of the supported indicators that compute and can be combined inside a signal rule. By default, they use a **length of 20** and **2 standard deviations**, but you can adjust those when you set up your experiment.  

A typical Bollinger Bands rule might look something like:  
> "Buy when price touches or crosses below the lower band, and sell when price touches or crosses above the upper band."  

You'd write this as a combination of conditions in a strategy signal. Because they're not a dedicated template like RSI or SMA, you'll need to build the rule yourself (which gives you more flexibility).  

So go ahead—just tell me the rule you're thinking of, and I'll help you set it up.

prose_judge.notes: The reply honestly states that Bollinger Bands are supported and can be used in a rule, without claiming any unsupported executable capability. It does not expose any raw runtime errors. The prose is appropriate for the ordinary conversation context.
